lines.note: Nikkei is defined as fine cinnamon. This opening headword matches the preceding page's catchword Nicqei, which is not repeated as extra running text there.

runs.text: Rol, ou papel de apontamentos que ſe

lines.note: Nikki is a daily record or paper of memoranda. The scan's c before q corrects OCR Nitqi; the relative clause continues on the next row.
The notes are made every day, completing the diary or daily-record definition. This short row belongs to Nicqi.
Nikkoo is explained by hi no hikari, sunlight. The scan's quǒ sequence and downward o mark are retained without replacing them with a normalized modern form.
Niku is equated with shishimura and glossed as flesh or meat. Xiximura is a Japanese synonym, not a Japanese word embedded within a Portuguese sentence.
This separate niku names an animal compared with an otter. The comparison is retained without assigning an unsupported modern species.
Nikugen denotes fleshly or external eyes. The Portuguese distinguishes ordinary bodily sight rather than merely repeating the meat sense of niku.

runs.text: Couſa odioſa, ou aborreciuel: junto eſte

lines.note: Nikui first means hateful or detestable. The following explanation introduces its grammatical use after verb stems.

runs.text: adiectiuo às raizes de muitos verbos faz ſer a

lines.note: The adjective can attach to the roots of many verbs. The Portuguese proceeds to explain the resulting sense of difficulty rather than hatred.
Such a combination makes the action difficult; shinikui is the example, something difficult to do. The divided Portuguese adjective continues below.
Completes difficultoſa deſe fazer, difficult to do. The vowel after c is u, not the OCR's a, while the close-set deſe remains unregularized.
Nikuu and nikusa are the adverbial and nominal forms associated with nikui. They are listed without separate translations.
Nikujiki is eating meat. The example begins at the right edge and continues the same compound on the next physical row.
Nikujiki wo yamuru means ceasing to eat meat. The Portuguese directly confirms that this is giving up meat-eating.

Nikumi, nikumu and its historical past form mean hating or detesting. The printed mark over the past ending's u points upward and is transcribed û, not the draft's grave; the principal part is not modernized to -nda.
Nikumi here is the noun hatred or aversion. It is a separate nominal entry despite sharing its spelling with the preceding verb stem.
Nikuminji and its principal forms give another verb for hating. The final Portuguese o- continues as odio below.
Completes odio, hatred. The upright S. marks written usage and is not part of the italic gloss. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Nikunikuto is an adverb expressing hateful or hostile manner. The alternative Portuguese paraphrase follows on the next row.
Com odio, with hatred, completes the adverbial definition. It is not a new headword or an omitted longer sentence.
Nikusabi is explained by the nautical expression obras mortas, the vessel's upperworks. The gloss concerns ship structure, not literally dead objects.
Nikusashi is cross-related to the preferred form nikutasu by Meliùs. The gloss begins the sense of overcooking; the scan has a comma after Meliùs, whose grave accent is preserved.

runs.text: zer a couſa atè ſe danar.

lines.note: Completes cozer a cousa até se danar: cooking something until it is spoiled. The verb does not mean ordinary cooking without this excessive result.
Nikutai means the body. The initial is N, not OCR X, and the short Portuguese gloss is complete on this row.
Nikutashi refers back to nikusashi for the overcooking sense. Vide is the italic editorial cross-reference, while the Japanese forms remain upright.
Nikutei denotes something that causes annoyance or aversion. The example below applies this to offensive things said by a person.
Nikutei wo yuu hito is a person who says objectionable things. The relative clause of the Portuguese translation continues below.

runs.text: couſas que cauſão aborrecimento, ou molestia.

lines.note: The things said cause aversion or annoyance. The scan supports couſas rather than OCR coaſas; the printed historical molestia is not modernized or accented editorially.
Nikuteina is the adjectival form, describing something objectionable or detestable. It follows the noun and its example as a separate entry.
Nikuteini is the associated adverbial form. Adu. classifies it without repeating the preceding definition.
Nikushin here denotes hatred or aversion. The following entry has the same spelling but a different meaning.

The second nikushin means the body and is marked for written usage. The scan reads Corpo, not OCR Corço, so the entry is not an animal name; S. is upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Nikushiki denotes the body's colour or complexion. The brief Portuguese phrase differentiates it from the preceding word for the body itself.

runs.text: Noz noſcada que ſerue de me-

lines.note: Nikuzuku is nutmeg, here described for medicinal use. The doubled z is retained, and me- begins mezinha across the physical line break.
Completes mezinha, a medicine or remedy. The short row closes the nutmeg entry.
Nidashi means boiling something to extract its properties. The example substance begins comba- and continues below; the printed principal part ita is not expanded or regularized.

runs.text: lamas, &c. pera lhe chupar a virtude, &

lines.note: Completes the substance name combalamas and says that boiling extracts its efficacy and flavour. The final letter of lamas is read as s rather than OCR t; the botanical identity is not asserted.

Sabor closes the extraction-by-boiling gloss. At the far right, the printed parenthesis and fundida are displaced continuation material for Nidobuqi on the row below: silver melted twice. They remain on this physical row rather than being semantically relocated or lost in the OCR's fused ſahor.fundida.

runs.text: Laya de prata que he duas vezes

lines.note: Nidobuki is a kind of silver that has been melted twice. Its final Portuguese word fundida is printed at the far right of the preceding physical row and is represented there explicitly.
Nihon is Japan. The dictionary's f spelling and the Portuguese Iapão are preserved rather than modernized.

runs.text: Liuro em que estão eſcritas as cou-

lines.note: Nihongi is described as a book recording the affairs of Japan. The description continues across the following rows and should not be replaced with a modern bibliographic definition.

runs.text: ſas de Iapão deſde que ſe começou atè idade dos

lines.note: Completes cousas and traces the account from Japan's beginnings to the age of its kings. The temporal clause continues below.

runs.text: Reis, & deſdos Reis atè agora. ¶ Item,

lines.note: The dictionary extends the description from the kings to the present and introduces another sense with Item. The contracted deſdos and the locally printed accents are retained.

runs.text: Custume, ou leis que correm em Iapão.

lines.note: The additional sense is the customs or laws current in Japan. It belongs to the Nihongi entry rather than being a new headword.
Nigai means bitter. The Portuguese amargoſa gives the taste quality, anticipating the nominal forms below.
Nigasa is bitterness, and nigoo is the associated adverbial form. Their order and the downward o mark are preserved as printed.
Nigami denotes bitterness or bitter tastes. The unusual printed Portuguese Amargòs and its grave mark are retained rather than normalized to an expected modern noun.

runs.text: Couſa queſe estranha, ou de que

lines.note: Niganigashii describes something objectionable or distressing. The gloss's second alternative continues below; this is a figurative extension of bitterness.
Completes the description as something that causes distress or regret. It belongs to the adjective above.
Niganigashisa is the corresponding quality noun. The damaged vowel after the second g is read as a, in agreement with the surrounding adjective and adverb, rather than the OCR's e.
Niganigashuu supplies the associated adverbial form. The downward u mark is preserved rather than rewritten as a modern long-vowel spelling.
Nigari means feeling hurt or resentful about something. The Portuguese object of the feeling continues as cousa below.

runs.text: ſa que lhe dißerão, ou fizerão. ¶

lines.note: The hurt comes from something said or done to the person. Nigat- begins the past-form example nigatta on the next row.
Nigatta koto wo yuu means saying objectionable things. The translation characterizes them as inappropriate and continues with their effect on others.

runs.text: & que tocão, ou dão pena a outros.

lines.note: The words touch a sore point or cause others distress. This completes the example, not a new sense involving physical contact alone.

runs.text: O rirſe ſecamente não ſendo de co-

lines.note: Nigawarai is a dry or forced laugh, not coming from the heart. The Portuguese coração is divided across the next row.
Completes coração and supplies nigawarai wo suru, giving such a forced laugh. Idem refers to the preceding explanation.

runs.text: Homem que vai de ſobreſelente, ou

lines.note: Nigawari is a relief porter, a person accompanying the carrier as a substitute. The Portuguese explains this by his unladen status and ability to take a turn below.

runs.text: deſpejado pera ſe reuezar com o que leua o fato

lines.note: The relief man travels without a load so that he can alternate with the person carrying the baggage. The location of that load follows on the next row.
Completes carrying the baggage on one's back. The grave accent in às is visible and was missing from the draft.
Nigashi means letting someone or something escape. Its printed historical past ending aita is retained rather than modernized to -shita.
Nigoo is explained by sayuu, both sides, namely right and left. The right-side term in the Portuguese gloss is divided at the line end.
Completes direita and gives esquerda, left. Nigoo ni tsuranaru means lining up on both sides; the scan supports r in eſquerda, not OCR n.

runs.text: Porſe em fieira, ou por ordem dambas as par-

lines.note: The example is translated as taking position in a line or in order on both sides. The final partes continues below.
Completes partes, sides. The separate upright S. marks the expression as written usage. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

runs.text: Duas palauras. i, Tornar a dizer.

lines.note: Nigon literally gives two words or utterances and is explained here as saying something again. The example below uses a negative commitment not to repeat oneself.
Nigon to moosumai means that one will not say it a second time. Portuguese Não ei de tornar begins the corresponding future refusal and continues below.
Completes tornar a dizer, to say again. The scan has dizer with i, not OCR dezer.
Nigorakashi means making something turbid. The second letter is i, not the draft's u, and the historical past ending aita is retained.

This is the related nigorashi verb for clouding a liquid. The scan itself appears to omit i after N, so Ngoraxi is preserved as a printed anomaly; the past ending reads aita, not atta. Portuguese vinho begins at the right edge.
Completes vinho, wine, as an example alongside water of something that can be made cloudy. The row is a short continuation of Ngoraxi.

runs.text: Eſtar turua a agoa, ou vinho.

lines.note: Nigori is the intransitive verb for water or wine being turbid. The final word is wholly italic vinho; the OCR's mixed-type vinba is not Japanese material.

runs.text: O eſtar a agoa turua, ou enlodada.

lines.note: Nigori here is the noun for water's cloudiness or muddiness. It is separate from the preceding verb entry.

The figurative example toga no nigori ni somu concerns being stained by fault or sin. Permet. introduces the transferred sense. The mark over o is reduced to a small ink trace; the aligned draft's ô is retained rather than replacing it with an unmarked vowel on linguistic expectations alone.
Completes macular-se com peccado, becoming stained with sin. This confirms the figurative interpretation of the preceding Japanese example.

runs.text: Vinho brãco como turuo de Iapão.

lines.note: Nigorizake is Japanese liquor described as white and cloudy. The historical Portuguese vinho is the dictionary's category, not a claim that this is grape wine.
Nigoshi is another transitive verb for making something turbid. The printed past ending oita is retained as historical morphology.
Nige and its principal forms mean fleeing. The following quotation starts toru mono mo across the row boundary.
Toru mono mo toriayezu describes leaving without time to take anything; mina kachi hadashi nite says that everyone was on foot and barefoot. The comma after toriayezu is visible in the scan.

Yama ye nigeagaru completes the flight up into the mountains. The upright citation reads Chr. N., not the OCR's Chi. N.; Lib. begins the italic book reference without an inferred expansion of the abbreviated source title.

runs.text: 4. Sem poder tomar nada com preßa descal-

lines.note: Book 4 is followed by the translation: unable to take anything, they fled in haste and barefoot. The physical division descal-ços continues below; podertomar retains the close-set printed spacing.

runs.text: ços, & a pee ſe acolherão aos montes.

lines.note: Completes descalços and says that they took refuge in the mountains on foot. The scan supplies pee, with two e types, and separates the reflexive ſe; the draft's peſe obscured both.
Nigekakure means hiding while fleeing. The Portuguese combines flight and concealment, not merely departure from a place.
Nigechiri means fleeing in scattered directions. The Portuguese gives a second description of dispersal below.
Completes the scattering gloss with dispersal through different places. The final adjective is diuerſas, not OCR diuerſan; the historical treſmontandoſe is retained.

runs.text: Cabeça, que ſe toma naguerra dal-

lines.note: Nigekubi is a head taken in war from a fleeing person. The description of that person continues below, with dal- beginning dalgum.
The victim is someone in flight. Nigekubi wo to- introduces taking such a head; fugindo is recovered from the OCR's fuginao.

runs.text: Tomar algũa cabeça deſtes, o que ſe tem

lines.note: Completes toru and translates taking a head from one of these fugitives. The scan supports Tomar and deſtes, replacing the OCR's Poniar and deſies.
The dictionary says that this is regarded as showing little valour. This assessment belongs to the historical gloss, not an added judgement by the reviewer.
Nigekuzushi describes fleeing hastily while breaking formation. The printed past ending uita is a historical form and agrees with the example below.
The flight is disorderly and scattered. Vt introduces an illustration comparing the fugitives to leaves carried by the wind.
Kaze ni konoha no chiru yoo ni compares the action to leaves scattering in the wind. Muramura names the settlements or their groups collectively, as the Portuguese translation confirms.
Batto nigekuzuita describes their sudden disorderly flight. Tac. is the upright citation label; the Portuguese translation begins with the comparison to leaves.

runs.text: que leua o vento todas as pouoações ſe derão à-

lines.note: The wind carries the leaves, and all the settlements take to flight. Enlarged reinspection recovers the faint second o in pouoações and supports ſe derão à-; the next page continues preßa a fugir. The damaged word and ending remain nonblocking reading caveats, with the physical terminal hyphen retained.
